name: Low-glycemic diet (for acne)
lead: A low-glycemic diet (low-GI or low-glycemic-load diet) is an eating pattern built around carbohydrates that are digested slowly, such as legumes, whole grains, most fruit and non-starchy vegetables, in place of white bread, sugary drinks and sweets. People adopt it to get clearer, less oily skin: the idea is that steadier glucose and insulin levels reduce the hormonal signals that drive oil production and clogged pores, so fewer breakouts appear.[1][4][9]

The glycemic index, introduced by David Jenkins and colleagues in 1981, ranks carbohydrate foods against pure glucose, and glycemic load adjusts that ranking for portion size.[2] The link between diet and acne was long treated as folklore; dermatologists in the late twentieth century commonly told patients that food did not matter. A series of papers from 2002 onward, including population observations in non-Western societies and small randomized trials, led reviewers to reopen the question.[8][9][10]

Randomized trials in young men and in men and women with acne have measured lesion counts, hormones and skin biopsies on low-glycemic-load diets, with reductions in lesion counts reported in studies lasting 10 to 12 weeks.[4][5][6] Other trials, including one that added the diet to topical treatment, did not find a difference in lesion counts between groups.[18] The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline focuses on drug and procedural treatments, while review articles describe diet as an area of active research.[17][19]

chain: Lower glucose and insulin swings, lower IGF-1 in trials
angle.text: People adopt a low-glycemic diet to reduce acne lesions and oiliness so their skin looks clearer. In trials, participants eating low-glycemic-load diets showed lower lesion counts and, in one study, smaller sebaceous glands on biopsy.

infobox: Fewer acne lesions, less oily skin

paras: The glycemic index rates carbohydrate-containing foods by their effect on blood glucose over two hours relative to a reference such as glucose; foods scoring 55 or less are classed as low, 56 to 69 as medium and 70 or more as high.[2] Glycemic load multiplies GI by the grams of carbohydrate in a serving and divides by 100, so it reflects how much of a food is eaten as well as how fast it is digested.[2]

A low-glycemic diet for acne emphasizes low-GI carbohydrates and reduces refined, high-GI items such as white bread, sweets and sugary beverages. No single standard version exists. Trial diets have ranged from low-GI carbohydrate combined with higher protein (about 25 percent of energy from protein and 45 percent from low-GI carbohydrate in the 2007 trials) to plain low-glycemic-load advice and counseling.[4][5][22]

The approach overlaps with other dietary patterns discussed for skin, including Mediterranean-style eating, higher fruit and vegetable intake, omega-3 fatty acid intake and reduced dairy; reviews treat these as separate but related lines of inquiry.[16][17]

sections.h: Origins and history of the diet-acne question
paras: Before the 1960s, certain foods such as chocolate and fatty foods were widely thought to worsen acne. Later studies, including two small and now old trials, led dermatology to regard such links as myths for several decades.[9][10] A 2005 systematic review of lay beliefs about diet, face-washing and sunlight found surprisingly little evidence for or against dietary factors in acne management and noted that much of what existed had methodological limitations.[11]

In 2002, Loren Cordain and colleagues published observations in Archives of Dermatology on two non-Westernized populations. Among 1,200 Kitavan Islanders of Papua New Guinea, including 300 aged 15 to 25, no case of acne was observed; among 115 Aché hunter-gatherers of Paraguay, none was seen over 843 days.[8] The authors attributed the contrast with the 79 to 95 percent adolescent prevalence in Westernized societies mainly to environmental factors rather than genetics, and Cordain's 2005 review set out how diet could influence the proximate causes of acne.[8][10]

In 2007, Robyn Smith and colleagues in Australia reported randomized trials of low-glycemic-load diets, and a 2010 review by Bowe, Joshi and Shalita concluded that dermatologists could no longer dismiss a diet-acne association and that evidence for a role of high-glycemic-load diets was compelling, while noting the lack of large randomized trials.[4][5][9]

Proponents and some clinicians propose that high-glycemic meals produce larger insulin responses, which raise IGF-1 and androgen activity, increasing sebum production and follicular blockage.[1][10] Wikipedia notes that androgens and IGF-1 both appear to be required for acne, since acne does not develop in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome or in Laron syndrome, which involves low IGF-1.[1]

Bodo Melnik and colleagues have described a related model in which insulin and IGF-1 signalling, together with branched-chain amino acids and certain fats from a Western-style diet, activate the nutrient-sensing kinase mTORC1 and suppress the transcription factor FoxO1, shifting sebaceous glands toward greater lipid production. In this model, three food classes promote acne: high-glycemic carbohydrates, milk and dairy products, and saturated and trans fats with low omega-3 intake.[12][23]

Cordain's framework lists five proximate causes of acne that diet might influence: keratinocyte proliferation in the pore, incomplete shedding of cells from the duct, androgen-driven sebum production, colonization by Cutibacterium (formerly Propionibacterium) acnes and inflammation.[10]

A 2007 randomized trial in 43 males aged 15 to 25 compared a diet of about 25% protein and 45% low-GI carbohydrate with a carbohydrate-dense control diet for 12 weeks. Lesion counts fell more in the low-glycemic-load group, which also lost more weight and improved insulin sensitivity; the authors noted that weight loss may have contributed.[4] A second 2007 randomized, investigator-masked trial of 43 male patients with a high-protein, low-glycemic-load diet reported greater lesion reduction, a lower free androgen index and higher IGFBP-1, again with weight loss as a possible contributor.[5] A 2008 analysis from the same program in 31 participants examined sebum and reported a change in the saturated to monounsaturated fatty acid ratio of skin surface triglycerides in the low-glycemic-load group compared with controls.[13]

A 2012 Korean randomized trial in 32 patients with mild to moderate acne ran 10 weeks. The low-glycemic-load group had fewer inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesions, and biopsies showed smaller sebaceous glands, less inflammation and lower SREBP-1 and IL-8 expression.[6] A 2018 randomized trial in 66 adults with moderate to severe acne found that IGF-1 fell significantly after two weeks on a low GI/GL diet, while glucose, insulin and body composition did not differ; the authors called for longer studies.[7]

A 2019 randomized trial in 84 patients with grade 1 to 3 acne compared 2.5 percent benzoyl peroxide gel with a low-glycemic-load diet against the gel alone for 12 weeks. Both groups had significant reductions in lesion counts with no statistically significant difference between them, although body mass index and insulin resistance fell in the diet group; the authors noted that the gel itself may have contributed to improvement in both arms.[18] Later 12-week randomized trials in moderate acne and in women aged 15 to 35 have also been published.[21][22]

Observational studies describe associations rather than effects of an intervention. In the NutriNet-Santé cross-sectional study of 24,452 French adults, current acne was associated with fatty and sugary products (adjusted odds ratio 1.54), sugary beverages (1.18) and milk (1.12).[15] In a cross-sectional study of 248 New York young adults, dietary factors were compared across self-reported acne severity groups.[20] A Nurses' Health Study II analysis of 47,355 women linked recalled high-school milk intake, including skim milk, to physician-diagnosed severe teenage acne.[14]

Reviews summarize this literature. A 2021 systematic review of 2009 to 2020 research identified 53 studies, including 11 interventional trials, and reported that high-GI/GL foods, dairy and fatty foods were among acne-associated factors, while fruit, vegetables and fatty acids were associated with lower acne.[17] A 2021 review in the American Journal of Clinical Dermatology states that individuals with acne who consume low-glycemic-load diets have reduced lesions compared with those on high-glycemic-load diets.[16] Many larger low-GI trials have studied diabetes and weight rather than skin, for example a meta-analysis of low-GI diets in diabetes management.[3]

Dairy is the most frequently studied companion topic. Wikipedia reports weak observational evidence linking milk to more frequent and severe acne, and a proposed role for whey protein, bovine IGF-1 and androgen precursors; it states that evidence was insufficient as of 2014 to recommend milk restriction.[1] A 2021 review suggests whey proteins' insulin-stimulating effects may matter more than fat content.[16]

The same Wikipedia article states that available evidence does not support a link between chocolate or salt and acne severity, while the 2021 systematic review lists chocolate among associated factors, showing that interpretations differ across sources.[1][17]

Wikipedia lists several caveats: GI values change with ripeness and cooking, individual responses vary from day to day, GI ignores portion size and insulin response, and some low-GI foods such as chocolate cake and ice cream are not otherwise considered healthy.[2] A 2023 Cochrane review, cited there, found low-GI or low-GL diets did not produce more weight loss in overweight adults than other approaches.[2]

Researchers of the acne trials point to the difficulty of separating the diet's glycemic properties from accompanying changes such as weight loss, higher protein intake and reduced energy intake, and to the short durations and small samples of existing studies.[4][5][7][18]

In appearance-focused communities, a low-sugar or low-glycemic approach is one of the common non-drug steps discussed alongside topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide and sunscreen, usually framed as a way to support skin clarity rather than replace dermatological treatment. Members often pair it with cutting sugary drinks, adding protein, and tracking skin changes over several weeks, reflecting the 10 to 12 week duration of most trials.[4][6]

Variants discussed online include low-carbohydrate and ketogenic eating, dairy avoidance, and the Mediterranean pattern; reviews classify these separately from low-glycemic-load interventions that were tested in the acne trials.[16][17]

timeline.event: David Jenkins and colleagues introduce the glycemic index.[2]
Cordain and colleagues report no acne among Kitavan Islanders and Aché hunter-gatherers.[8]
A systematic review finds little high-quality evidence either way on diet and acne; Cordain publishes a review on diet's role in acne.[10][11]
Two randomized trials of low-glycemic-load diets in young men with acne are published.[4][5]
Bowe, Joshi and Shalita review diet and acne and conclude dermatologists can no longer dismiss the link.[9]
Korean randomized trial reports lower lesion counts and smaller sebaceous glands on a low-glycemic-load diet.[6]
Melnik reviews mTORC1 and FoxO1 signalling as a link between Western diet and acne.[12]
Two-week randomized trial reports lower IGF-1 in adults with moderate to severe acne.[7]
Indian randomized trial of a low-glycemic-load diet added to benzoyl peroxide reports no between-group difference in lesion counts.[18]
Systematic review of 2009-2020 research identifies 53 diet-and-acne studies.[17]
AAD publishes updated acne guidelines centered on drug and procedural therapies.[19]

lore.intro: Skincare and fitness communities discuss glycemic control as a lever for skin, often alongside dairy, sugar and whey protein, citing the trials and reviews above.[9][17]

claims.claim: Cutting sugar and refined carbs clears acne
claims.believers: Proponents say breakouts follow high-sugar days and improve after switching to low-GI foods, pointing to the 12-week trials showing lower lesion counts.[4][6]
claims.experts: Randomized trials in small groups reported fewer lesions on low-glycemic-load diets, while one trial adding the diet to benzoyl peroxide found no between-group difference.[4][6][18]

claims.claim: Insulin and IGF-1 spikes drive oily skin
claims.believers: Advocates describe a chain from blood glucose to insulin, IGF-1, androgens and sebum.[10]
claims.experts: A two-week trial found lower IGF-1 on a low GI/GL diet, and Wikipedia notes that androgens and IGF-1 appear necessary for acne; the pathway is described as proposed.[1][7]

claims.claim: Acne is a disease of Western diet
claims.believers: Cordain's 2002 observation of no acne among Kitavans and Aché is cited as support.[8]
claims.experts: The authors concluded environmental factors, not only genetics, likely explain the difference; the study was observational and did not isolate diet.[8]

claims.believers: Many members avoid milk or whey, citing studies linking skim milk to acne.[14]
claims.experts: Observational studies report associations, and Wikipedia describes the evidence as weak and insufficient to recommend milk restriction.[1][15]

claims.believers: Some say chocolate triggers their skin.
claims.experts: Wikipedia states evidence does not support a link between chocolate and acne severity, while a 2021 review lists chocolate as an associated factor.[1][17]

claims.believers: Some members hope to avoid drugs entirely by changing diet.
claims.experts: The 2024 AAD guideline recommends drug and procedural therapies, and reviews describe diet as complementary research.[16][19]

claims.claim: Weight loss from the diet explains the results
claims.believers: Skeptical members point out that the trial groups lost weight.
claims.experts: Authors of the 2007 trials noted weight loss may have contributed to the improvements.[4][5]

card.summary: Eating low-GI carbs to calm acne: the one diet tweak with some trial support, though the evidence is modest.
card.note: Glycemic index values vary with ripeness, cooking and the individual, and diet is not a substitute for medical acne care.

quick.overview:
A low-glycemic diet swaps fast-digesting carbohydrates such as white bread, sugary drinks and sweets for slower ones such as legumes, whole grains and most vegetables. In looksmaxxing and skincare circles it is discussed as a way to reduce acne without drugs.

According to Wikipedia's acne article, several randomized and non-randomized studies have reported that lower-glycemic-load diets reduced acne severity, and dermatologists commonly suggest a diet low in simple sugars. The overall body of evidence is described as emerging rather than settled.
quick.mechanism: The proposed mechanism is that high-glycemic meals raise blood glucose and insulin, which is thought to increase IGF-1 and androgen activity, and in turn sebum production and comedone formation. Androgens and IGF-1 are both considered important in acne biology.
quick.risks: A low-GI eating pattern is generally an ordinary dietary approach with no specific safety concerns identified in the sources. Glycemic index is an imperfect measure: some foods with a low GI are high in fat or sugar, and values vary between individuals and preparations.
